Academic stuff
I’m an Assistant Professor of Global Change in the Integrative Biology Department at the University of South Florida - St. Petersburg. I’m a macroecologist and community ecologist who works across taxa (primarily focusing on plants and terrestrial vertebrates) using both ecological and evolutionary approaches with strong informatics and computational components. I’m a big believer in working collaboratively, which benefits from the integration of diverse perspectives and multiple skill sets.

title: Lab Members
text:
Michiel (Mich) Pillet





Academic stuff
I’m a Postdoctoral Research Scholar in the Department of Integrative Biology at the University of South Florida and an Associate Researcher in the Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology at the University of Arizona. I consider myself a conservation ecologist specializing in climate change impacts on biodiversity, with a focus on cacti and succulents. My research integrates ecological theory, evolutionary approaches, species distribution modeling, and other quantitative methods to inform conservation planning and policy. I collaborate widely with academic partners and conservation stakeholders, and believe strongly in the importance of public engagement and science communication.

I’m obsessed with cacti, objectively the best plant family. I also operate a conservation nursery, Prickly Prospects.

title: Lab Members
text:
Mac Grosscup





Academic stuff
I am a Master’s Student in the Conservation Biology program at the University of South Florida – St. Petersburg. Plant ecology is one of my primary scientific interests, specifically in the Neotropics. I am curious about how plants broadly respond to global change, as well as how rare or underrepresented taxa reappear after disturbance events. I am particularly interested in examining these phenomena through the lens of trait evolution.

Email: jgrosscup@usf.edu

Outside of the Lab
I have an extensive collection of tropical epiphytes from families like Araceae, Orchidaceae, and Apocynaceae. I also love cooking recipes from many different global cuisines!

title: Lab Members
text:
Alyssa Diodato





Academic stuff
I’m a Master’s Student in Conservation Biology at the University of South Florida- St. Petersburg. I have a strong background in horticulture for the purpose of habitat restoration, and an interest in plant ecology insights that can be applied to practice. I am interested in how climate change or land use patterns may affect suitable habitat ranges as well as looking at specific responses in plants themselves, such as germination time. I hope my work can someday provide practitioners with better insights to create more resilient ecosystems.

Email: adiodato@usf.edu

Outside of the Lab
I love playing DND with friends, doing anything creative with my hands, and watching animated shows and movies. The temperate forests of the Northeast United States and the landscapes of Ireland both have a special place in my heart.

title: Prospective Students
text:
The Maitner Lab is looking for graduate students to join us in the Department of Integrative Biology at the University of South Florida – St. Petersburg. If you want to study ecology in Florida and you’re excited about biodiversity, plants, conservation, or using data to answer big questions, we’d love to hear from you.
We’re especially interested in students drawn to either (or both) of these approaches:

Data science and coding to address large-scale questions in macroecology and biodiversity, such as aggregating and cleaning large datasets, mapping biodiversity, and modeling species distributions.
Field-based methods to address ecological or global-change questions, such as measuring plant traits and studying how communities respond to disturbance and climate change.

You don’t need to arrive with every skill. We care most that you are strongly self-motivated, curious, and full of your own ideas.

title: Prospective Students
text:
What we work on
Research in the lab centers on biodiversity patterns, conservation, and Open Science. Work is open to any group of organisms, but it tends to focus on plants. Current and recent topics include:

Plant functional traits and how they relate to the environment
Climate change impacts on biodiversity, including threatened cacti and succulents
Species range shifts and conservation planning
Biodiversity knowledge gaps and large-scale data integration (e.g., BIEN)
Open Science and research software in ecology

See Publications for our papers, and Lab Members to learn what current students and postdocs are working on.

title: Prospective Students
text:
Graduate programs
So far, graduate students in the lab have been in USF’s M.S. in Conservation Biology, which is offered only at the St. Petersburg campus. Key features:

Thesis-based. Students design and carry out their own research and are encouraged to publish it.
Two to three years is the typical time to finish.
Local partners include the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, the U.S. Geological Survey, and the USF College of Marine Science, all near campus.
Career paths for graduates include state and federal agencies, conservation organizations, environmental consulting, zoos, and Ph.D. programs.

Ph.D. students are also possible through USF’s doctoral programs on the Tampa campus, such as the Ph.D. in Integrative Biology (Ecology and Evolution concentration).

title: Prospective Students

Funding
Most graduate students in the lab are funded as Graduate Teaching Assistants. Current minimum stipends (as of fall 2026) for a 9-month, 0.50 FTE appointment:

Graduate Assistants also receive:

Tuition waivers. Students remain responsible for some university fees.
Subsidized health insurance. For 2026–27, USF pays $3,483 of the $4,267 annual premium for domestic students and the full premium for international students (USF HR).

These minimum stipends, tuition waiver eligibility, and health insurance subsidies are guaranteed by the collective bargaining agreement negotiated by USF’s graduate assistant union, Graduate Assistants United (GAU).
Please go in with your eyes open: USF stipends are low compared with the cost of living in the Tampa Bay area, and compared with other universities in the Association of American Universities (AAU). The M.S. stipend falls below the federal poverty line (Open Campus, 2025). The GAU continues to bargain for higher pay.
Because of this, we strongly encourage students to apply for external fellowships (such as the NSF Graduate Research Fellowship), and Brian is happy to help with applications.

title: Prospective Students
text:
How to apply

Email Brian first at bmaitner@usf.edu. Please include:

a short description of your research interests and why the lab is a good fit
your CV
any experience with coding, data analysis, or fieldwork (none is required, but tell us what you’ve done)

Talk with us. If there’s a good fit, we’ll set up a video call to talk about research ideas, the program, and the lab.
Apply to USF through the USF graduate application. Check the Integrative Biology graduate program page for current requirements and deadlines.

title: Prospective Students
text:
Life in St. Petersburg, Florida
USF St. Petersburg sits on the waterfront in downtown St. Petersburg, on Tampa Bay along Florida’s Gulf Coast. The campus is a short drive from USF’s main campus in Tampa. The campus is small, and the lab is collaborative, so students get plenty of one-on-one mentoring alongside a much larger university’s resources.

title: Maitner Lab
text:
Overview
The Maitner Lab is led by Dr. Brian Maitner in the Department of Integrative Biology at the University of South Florida – St. Petersburg. The focus of the lab is (primarily) on topics related to biodiversity, including quantifying and mapping biodiversity, understanding the drivers of biodiversity patterns and how biodiversity may be impacted by global changes, and working on making these findings relevant for decision makers. Work in the lab is open to any group of organisms, but tends to focus on plants (as they account for most of the biomass on Earth and their traits are primary drivers of terrestrial ecosystem functioning). We practice Open Science and take a highly collaborative and cooperative approach to research.


Research Areas

Biodiversity patterns
We study biodiversity patterns using both top-down and bottom-up approaches. With the top-down approach, we use data science to aggregate and clean existing data to ask questions at large spatial or taxonomic scales. For example, we’ve worked with our collaborators to assess knowledge gaps in plant data and shortfalls in plant conservation assessments, and have shown how database integration can lead to massive improvements in data availability. With the bottom-up approach, we focus on using field observations to understand biodiversity patterns and their correlates. For example, with our collaborators, we’ve worked on understanding environmental correlates of plant traits in China, Norway, Peru, and other locations. We also work on improving how trait-based ecology is done, including better incorporating uncertainty and advocating for best-practices in trait-based ecology.


Conservation
In addition to studying biodiversity patterns themselves, we’re interested in how that knowledge can be applied in a conservation setting. Knowing how biodiversity is distributed, and how it might be changing, is of critical importance for protecting biodiversity (and its contributions to people). For example, we’ve worked with colleagues to understand how climate change may be threatening cactus species and how we can design protected areas in response to species range shifts. We’ve also worked to asssess the impacts of fires on biodiversity in both the Amazon and Australia. We’re also interested in how global change drivers can be used as “unplanned experiments” to test ecological theories, for example testing community assembly theory using bird introductions.


Open Science
Open Science work in the lab includes both work focused on the development and dissemination of Open Science products and work focused on the impacts of Open Science. For example, we participate in the development and maintainance of multiple R packages, including BIEN, TNRS, GNRS, and Wallace 2. In terms of work focused on the impact of Open Science, we’ve published on the importance of Open Science in trait-based ecology, the need to incentivize software developers, and have shown how Open Science can improve citation rates.
For a full list of our papers, preprints, R packages, and datasets, see Publications.



Join the lab!
We’re currently looking for graduate students to join the lab. Students should be strongly self-motivated and full of ideas they’re interested in! In particular, we’re looking for students that have an interest in either (or both) of the following approaches: 1) using data wrangling and coding to address large-scale questions, or 2) using field-based methods to address ecological or global-change questions. See the Prospective Students page for details on how to apply, or email Brian if you’re interested.
